lesson.title: Close to the Truth vs. Close Together: Accuracy and Precision
lesson.summary: Accuracy describes how near a measurement is to the true value, while precision describes how consistently repeated measurements agree with each other, and understanding the difference is essential for judging whether an experimental result can be trusted.
lesson.body:
Accuracy and precision sound like synonyms in everyday conversation, but in chemistry they describe two distinct and independent properties of a set of measurements, and both matter when evaluating data collected as described in the Measurement unit. Accuracy describes how close a measured value is to the true or accepted value, the number you would get from a perfect instrument with no error at all. Precision describes how close a series of repeated measurements are to each other, regardless of whether that cluster of values sits anywhere near the true value. A measurement set can be accurate, precise, both, or neither, and recognizing which situation you are in changes how much you should trust the data.

A dartboard analogy makes the distinction concrete. If a thrower's darts land scattered widely across the board but happen to average out near the bullseye, the results are accurate on average but not precise, since individual throws disagree wildly with each other. If the darts cluster tightly together but land far from the bullseye, off in one corner, the results are precise but not accurate, since they agree with each other but not with the true target. Only when the darts cluster tightly around the bullseye itself are the results both accurate and precise, which is the goal of any well designed experiment.

In laboratory terms, imagine three students each measuring the mass of the same 10.00 g calibration weight five times on different balances. Student A gets 9.98, 10.02, 9.99, 10.01, and 10.00 g, values that are both tightly clustered and centered right on the true value of 10.00 g: accurate and precise. Student B gets 8.50, 8.52, 8.49, 8.51, and 8.50 g, values tightly clustered together, which shows good precision, but consistently far from the true 10.00 g, which shows poor accuracy, most likely because that balance was not properly zeroed or calibrated. Student C gets 9.10, 10.60, 9.80, 10.90, and 9.60 g, values that are scattered widely, showing poor precision, but that happen to average to about 10.00 g, showing accuracy on average even though no single measurement was very trustworthy on its own.

The difference between these two outcomes points to two different categories of experimental error. Poor precision, like Student C's scattered results, usually comes from random error, small unpredictable fluctuations from things like reading a scale slightly differently each time, air currents disturbing a balance, or reaction time in starting a stopwatch. Random error can be reduced by taking more measurements and averaging them, since scattered errors tend to cancel out over many trials. Poor accuracy despite good precision, like Student B's results, usually comes from systematic error, a consistent bias that pushes every measurement in the same direction, such as a miscalibrated instrument, a consistently misread meniscus, or a scale that was never zeroed. Systematic error cannot be fixed by averaging more trials, since every trial shares the same bias; it can only be corrected by identifying the flawed instrument or procedure and fixing or recalibrating it.

Recognizing which type of error is affecting a data set is a core skill for evaluating experimental results, and it sets up the next concept directly: percent error gives chemists a single numerical way to quantify exactly how accurate a measurement is compared to its accepted true value, turning this qualitative dartboard picture into a concrete, calculable number.
